items.title: Iowa Residents Told to Evacuate or Shelter in Place as U.S. Army Prepares to Detonate 10,000 Pounds of Lead Explosive
items.description: The U.S. Army plans to detonate 9,700 pounds of a lead-based explosive in southeast Iowa on Wednesday, despite concerns from environmental groups. The detonation is scheduled to go ahead at 10am EST on Wednesday morning at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, IA. This comes after a lawsuit was filed by the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter asking the federal appeals court to halt the plan. Two rapid, controlled detonations were initially scheduled to take place last Friday, but the plans were pushed to Wednesday due to a combination of public concern and weather optimization. Set to be detonated are 68 drums of degraded lead azide, adding up to roughly 9,700 pounds, which have become sensitive and unstable. It is the primary explosive used to initiate munitions A controlled detonation is now the only viable option, according to the Army’s Q&A page about the event. As lead azide degrades, it crystalizes and becomes sensitive to temperature changes, shock and friction, making it unsafe to move. There are chemical neutralization procedures, but the drums are too unstable for the physical manipulation this option requires, according to the Army. Loading... The army will detonated about 9,700 pounds of lead azide in Middletown, IA on Wednesday. Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images Inside the plan to detonate a lead-based explosive U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Region 7 Director Jim Macy wrote a letter to Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds , ensuring her that the EPA was working alongside the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the Department of Defense to ensure the controlled detonation was “conducted in the safest manner possible.” “All agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized,” Macy wrote in the letter, according to the Iowa Capital Dispatch . An updated public safety advisory shared by the Army on Tuesday shared the agency’s plans to make the detonation as safe as possible. The lead azide will be detonated in earth-covered magazines, which are built for the purposes of holding ammunition and explosives, and are reinforced. Additional physical barriers made of sand, a “water wall,” gel blocks, and aqueous foam barriers will be in place to contain particle dispersion, absorb thermal energy, and reduce airborne particulate dispersal. These measures, as well as drone surveillance of lead levels, are in place to track and minimize deposition outside the plant. Loading... The Army has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP". The Army has acknowledged that lead particles will impact communities outside the plant. It has defined an evacuation zone as a "5-mile cone extending southwest of IAAAP". Those in the evacuation zone will be provided short-term hotel lodging, food, water, and transportation as needed. It has also laid out recommendations for those outside the evacuation zone, such as sheltering in place, closing all windows and doors, and setting heating to recirculate and avoid pulling in air from outside. Loading... US army maps show projected path of toxic dust from the Iowa detonation. Environmental concerns over the detonation Still, environmental groups are concerned about the lead plum, which they say could spread 100 miles, depending on weather conditions. "The EPA itself admits that there is no safe level of lead exposure for humans," said Michael Schmidt , General Counsel at the Iowa Environmental Council, in a press release shared with Realtor.com. "When our federal government makes decisions that result in a potentially toxic plume of lead dust that could cover much of southeastern Iowa, Iowans deserve to know that every available alternative was considered before choosing this method of disposal." The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, Iowa Chapter, were only made aware of the unprecedented detonation plan early last week, initially scheduled for Friday. In response, the groups filed a lawsuit on Thursday challenging the permit that the EPA issued the Army. Loading... The public and local lawmakers were initially not made aware of the controlled detonation, a senior attorney says. Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images “Based on the information that was made public at the time, which was very little information, there were serious concerns about the effectiveness of the public notification and the information being put out to protect the public,” Thien Chau , a senior attorney at Earth Justice, told Realtor.com. “There were serious concerns about the mitigations measures in place to reduce the impact as well as to properly do remediation and cleanup and address any harm that people may face from the impact of the detonation.” Many local lawmakers were not made aware of the controlled detonation either, and were only informed about the plans and risk once the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra club told them, despite the widespread impact on surrounding communities, according to Chau. “That’s why we filed the lawsuit : to make sure that all the information and resources and capabilities that could be provided were provided to the people potentially impacted by this,” said Chau. “Since that filing, a lot of things have happened. items.title: New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft
items.description: New home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB's November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market's current state and foreseeable-future direction. According to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago. October's better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey's margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month. “A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement. New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction . The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September's 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier. October's sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn't erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market. Warning signs flash Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis. For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October. NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic. "Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand," Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today's new home sales release. "Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand." A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country's largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data. Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes , Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in new orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand. Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold, Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll's luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures. Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices. “As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28. Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton , acknowledged that October was another challenging month. “Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we've seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we'd anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29. Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October's sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision. “Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi said, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.” Related More: Homebuilders New Home Sales U.S. Census Bureau

items.title: Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?
items.description: Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot , low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what's happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs. Purchase apps and weekly demand grows As we've discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since. Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week. Purchase application data , on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization. Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down big, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December. New home sales beat estimates New home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it's still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates. One positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long. As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%. If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year's — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday! Related More:

items.title: Colorado first responders can now get state home mortgage help
items.description: A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn't look like a typical candidate for state housing help. In Colorado, if that borrower is a firefighter, emergency medical technician or police officer, the person now qualifies. The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority launched a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers. CHFA Colorado Champions uses a new state law that raises income limits for eligible borrowers. Colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers. The goal is to give them more chances to live near where they serve. Maryland, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Texas, Florida and South Carolina also offer similar programs. Earlier this month, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont announced a new homeownership assistance program for first responders. It offers up to $25,000 in forgivable down payment and closing cost assistance. The program stems from a law Lamont signed this year. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them,” Lamont said in a statement. State housing help arrives in a softening market CHFA Colorado Champions arrives as the housing market weakens, following several years of zoning and regulatory reform. Colorado's single-family housing market has been steadily cooling since spring, according to HousingWire Intelligence data through Nov. 20. Inventory peaked in September and has barely eased, while median list prices have fallen since July. Homes are also taking longer to sell, with days on market rising since late July and price reductions staying elevated. The latest weekly figures show no reversal, with single-family homes taking a median 91 days to sell, up from 84. The median single-family list price is $599,000, and about 48% of single-family listings carry price cuts, the data show. Lawmakers have spent years trying to improve affordability, mostly by loosening local land-use rules. In 2024, Gov. Jared Polis signed laws requiring more density near transit and clearing the way for accessory dwelling units. The package also removed some parking minimums for urban multifamily housing and lifted limits on unrelated people living together. A law Polis signed this year requires towns with more than 2,000 people to allow housing on certain small parcels. Eligible land belongs to school districts, colleges, transit districts, housing authorities and qualifying nonprofits. The law takes effect Dec. 31, 2027, while lot-size bills failed in the Legislature this year. How Colorado Champions works Senate Bill 26-053, a bipartisan law, raised CHFA's mortgage income limits to 110% of standard guidelines. That allows eligible borrowers earning up to $196,810 a year to qualify. The program offers a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage. The program covers down payment and closing costs up to the lesser of $25,000 or 4% of the first mortgage. Borrowers apply through a CHFA participating lender. The aid is a second mortgage. Repayment is deferred until the term ends, the first mortgage is paid off, or the borrower sells, refinances or moves. CHFA Executive Director Thomas Bryan said in a statement that first responders keep communities safe. Many can't afford local homes, he added. “They should be able to live where they serve,” Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, one of the law’s sponsors, said in a statement. Related More: Affordability mortgage

items.title: Better signs agreement with mortgage servicer to grow HELOC volume
items.description: Better Home & Finance Holding Co. signed an agreement with an unnamed mortgage servicer to offer home equity lines of credit (HELOCs) and home equity loans to existing borrowers, expanding its lead-generation channels as the company continues its turnaround efforts. The agreement, announced Tuesday in the company's Week 7 Better 2.0 scorecard, is expected to provide a lower-cost customer acquisition channel. Since its Week 6 scorecard on Nov. 17, Better has identified additional efficiencies across its corporate organization that are expected to generate a total of $38.97 million in annualized savings. The company also reported $770,000 in additional annualized savings from mortgage operations. Better said it plans to pursue another $1.5 million in vendor-related reductions by Dec. 1. The company is working toward a broader cost savings target of $64.2 million. “ HELOC volume with our partners continues to grow each week, four more brokerages are lined up to join our wholesale platform, and two new partnerships are set to launch. At the same time, we're moving toward a signed agreement to sell Birmingham Bank , which will let us focus fully on our U.S. business,” said Vishal Garg , Better's founder and head of product, platform and innovation. The company has received five term sheets for about $50 million in debt financing tied to the proposed sale of the bank and is continuing discussions with prospective financing partners. The company said its AI-powered HELOC partnership with a large existing customer is live, with volume increasing weekly. Better is also preparing a multichannel campaign to expand the product through its wholesale platform and onboard additional brokerages. Four more mortgage brokerages are in the pipeline to join the platform. Two previously announced partnerships — with a rental credit management platform and a home inspection company — are expected to launch early next week. Better is also advancing discussions with three other major partners and a previously revived large-scale partnership, its release stated. Related More: Better HELOCs Mortgage Servicing

items.title: Blatstein Lines Up Refi Of North Philly Shopping Center After Loan Maturity
items.description: The financing underpinning a North Philadelphia shopping center undergoing a partial residential conversion is up in the air, but the borrower said there will be more certainty soon. Google Maps The Shops at Avenue North The $27M loan for The Shops at Avenue North, just south of Temple University ’s main campus, has been transferred to special servicing after it matured last month, according to Morningstar Credit . The 94K SF property at 1600 N. Broad St., 40% of which is occupied by an AMC Theatres location, is owned by Tower Investments . “It’s being refinanced before the end of the year,” Tower CEO Bart Blatstein told Bisnow on Wednesday. “The payoff statement was requested a while back” The borrower has been working on a refinancing since July as the maturity approached, but there was still no term sheet as of Oct. 13, according to commentary from special servicer Rialto Capital Advisors . Blatstein declined Bisnow ’s request for more details about the upcoming refinancing deal. Occupancy at the shopping center was 100% when Deutsche Bank originated the loan in 2018. Temple used to lease space at the property for a gym, but it has since departed. The owner is working to convert that section of the building into 24 studio apartments set to deliver before the start of the upcoming school year in August 2027, Blatstein said. Enrollment at Temple fell by 26% to just under 30,000 students between 2017 and last year, according to the university . Greater Philadelphia's retail market has shown signs of strength: It had a vacancy rate of 4.5% last quarter, down 10 basis points year-over-year, according to a report from Marcus & Millichap . Asking rents grew 2.9% over the same period and are expected to reach $21.10 per SF by the end of the year, following declines in 2024 and 2025. The Shops at Avenue North isn't the only property where Blatstein is in the midst of financial maneuvering. His Showboat Hotel in Atlantic City is facing potential foreclosure proceedings over a pair of CMBS loans totaling approximately $48M. Investors in June sought a court-ordered sheriff’s sale to satisfy the unpaid balance on the loans, the Philadelphia Business Journal reported . Last month, Blatstein proposed taking out a $21.5M personal loan in an effort to resolve the matter. items.title: Vornado To Cash Out $575M In Stake Sale Of 90 Park Ave.
items.description: Vornado Realty Trust has agreed to sell a 49% stake in 90 Park Ave . in a deal that values that office tower at $722.5M, or $755 per SF. San Francisco-based investment firms Sixth Street Partners and DivcoWest are buying into the 956K SF building, which takes up the full western blockfront of Park Avenue at East 40th Street. Vornado Realty Trust The nearly 1M SF office tower at 90 Park Ave. Vornado will retain a majority interest in the property and continue to oversee management and leasing. The property is unencumbered, but the newly formed joint venture plans to obtain a nonrecourse loan of at least $500M tied to the asset. Vornado expects to receive net proceeds of approximately $575M from the transaction, the REIT announced in a press release Tuesday. The deal is expected to close by the end of the year. Newmark 's Adam Spies , Josh King and Adam Doneger represented Sixth Street Partners, while Eastdil Secured Savills ' Gary Phillips and Will Silverman represented Vornado. The office portion of the tower is fully leased, according to Vornado’s third-quarter earnings report . However, Alston & Bird, which occupies approximately 123K SF across multiple floors, inked a lease earlier this year to relocate to 170K SF at Harbor Group International ’s 51 W. 52nd St. Finding a replacement is unlikely to be an issue. Grand Central’s vacancy rate is among the lowest in the city, at 16.6%, according to Cushman & Wakefield . Large, contiguous blocks of space are especially rare. Although the building has a Park Avenue address, it is south of Grand Central Terminal and therefore doesn't qualify as part of the prized submarket. Vornado’s 350 Park Ave ., being constructed for hedge fund Citadel with a $3.3B loan , does. Average weighted rents at 90 Park Ave. are $87 per SF, according to Vornado's Q3 earnings supplemental report , above the $76.83-per-SF asking rent for all offices. The tower’s other major tenant is PwC , which leases 240K SF . MassMutual and Glencore also fill roughly 45K SF each. The building’s base is 96% occupied, with Citibank and Starbucks as its largest retail tenants. Vornado has greatly benefited from New York City’s market recovery, which leads the country. It signed tenants to 1.1M SF of leases through the first nine months of the year at an average initial rent of $113.09 per SF. Last year, Chairman and CEO Steven Roth expressed interest in selling assets elsewhere to focus on the well-performing properties in the city. items.title: Investors Face Total Loss On Portland Hilton Hotels With 83% Value Drop
items.description: The holders of bonds backing two Hilton hotels in downtown Portland, Oregon, are expected to face a complete loss after the properties’ valuation plummeted. Google Maps The Hilton Portland Downtown The Hilton Portland Downtown and the Duniway Portland, which sit just steps away from each other and total 782 rooms, have a new appraisal of $58M, Morningstar Credit reported last month. That appraisal, completed in July, represents an 83% drop from their $340.3M valuation seven years prior, when a note to refinance the properties was packaged into a commercial mortgage-backed security, Bloomberg reported this week. The new appraisal means that the value placed on these assets is less than a quarter of the $240M in debt on them. Meanwhile, $53M in advances have been executed to cover costs associated with the properties, meaning that any sale at the current valuation would result in a total loss for bondholders, according to Bloomberg. Such a sale is not imminent, according to special servicer commentary from SitusAMC Holdings Corp. filed with Morningstar Credit, with marketing “on hold pending an improvement of the market.” “The Portland hospitality market is distressed,” the commentary noted. It notes that the February sale of the Portland Marriott for $30M — a 63% discount from its 2013 price — was the city's first sale post-Covid. But a meeting with the Portland travel bureau signaled “green shoots for increased demand” coming to the city in 2027 and 2028, SitusAMC wrote. The Hilton Portland Downtown and the Duniway Portland were formerly owned by affiliates of Brookfield Asset Management , which purchased them in 2015 for $270M, according to Bloomberg. The affiliates refinanced the loan in 2019 when they were repackaged as a CMBS. But in 2020, BAM's affiliates defaulted on their mortgage, and in 2023, the properties were foreclosed on, leaving them in the hands of the bondholders. Brookfield spent $36.6M on renovations to the properties following its acquisition, according to Bloomberg, citing the bond's prospectus. During the first half of the year, the Portland hotels had a negative net operating income of $410K, according to Morningstar Credit. During that time, the properties made nearly as much in revenue as they spent in operating expenses: about $36M came in, while approximately just as much went out. That 100% operating expense ratio compares to a 90% ratio for all of 2025 and 80% during both of the prior years. items.title: The Fed is likely to raise rates in December. What it means for your holiday spending
items.description: Read more CNBC personal finance coverage Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says The Fed is likely to raise rates in December. What it means for your holiday spending Trump administration proposes rule that could curb ESG investing in 401(k)s CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The central bank sets the federal funds rate, the interest rate at which banks borrow and lend to one another overnight. Although consumers do not pay that rate directly, changes to the federal funds rate ripple through many of the borrowing costs they face every day. When the Fed raises rates, borrowing becomes more expensive, helping to slow economic activity and ease inflation. But as a result, Americans may face higher costs for mortgages, auto loans and credit cards, among other forms of debt. Credit card rates will rise Pressmaster | Istock | Getty Images Credit cards are particularly sensitive to Fed policy because most carry variable interest rates. As the federal funds rate rises, so does the prime rate, which credit card issuers use as a benchmark. Card rates typically adjust within one or two billing cycles after the Fed adjusts its policy. That will come at a difficult time for consumers. Not only are Americans heading into the fourth quarter carrying a record $1.29 trillion in credit card debt, but 66% of consumers with unsecured debt are still paying off last year's holiday purchases, according to a recent survey of 2,000 U.S. adults by National Debt Relief, a debt settlement firm. "What's particularly concerning is that many Americans are heading into this holiday season still paying off debt from the last one," Peter Beaugard, chief revenue officer at National Debt Relief, said in a written statement. "When holiday spending turns into debt that carries over year after year, it can create a cycle that becomes increasingly difficult to break." With affordability already stretched , higher borrowing costs could put additional pressure on household budgets, though the impact is unlikely to be felt evenly, experts said. "Higher-income households that pay their card balance in full won't see any significant change in what ends up under the tree," said Cristian deRitis, deputy chief economist at Moody's Analytics. "Lower-income and younger households already leaning on credit cards will feel the pinch," he said. Higher interest rates are intended to cool demand. As borrowing becomes more expensive and debt burdens grow, households may have little choice but to pull back on spending in the months ahead, experts say. That may include holiday spending, though consumers may first opt to look for savings elsewhere, experts said. "Some spending will be trimmed, but consumers will likely cut elsewhere before they cut gifts," deRitis said. Car loans and mortgage rates remain elevated Other borrowing costs are affected more indirectly by the central bank. However, anyone shopping for a car or home this holiday season could still be impacted by the Fed's next move. Auto loan rates , for example, are tied to several factors, including the Fed's benchmark. Even as new-car APRs hover above 7% and car prices remain elevated, December is traditionally a good time to buy a vehicle as dealers look to clear inventory before the end of the year, according to Ivan Drury, director of insights at Edmunds. "Normally, waiting for December APR deals comes with a tradeoff: shrinking inventory of current-model-year vehicles, where discounts would provide the most value," he said. This year, however, buyers face an added hurdle. Auto loan interest rates remain near historic highs — and could go even higher — while the average transaction price has climbed above $50,000. A home for sale in Los Angeles, California, Nov. 20, 2026. Justin Sullivan | Getty Images Alternatively, 15- and 30-year fixed mortgage rates don't move with the Fed's benchmark rate. Instead, they generally track long-term Treasury yields , which remain elevated. As a result, 30-year fixed mortgage rates have stayed above 7% since September, according to Mortgage News Daily , pushing the real estate sector into a deep freeze . watch now VIDEO 2:52 02:52 Frozen market hits homebuyers The Exchange "Now that we're entering the holiday season, many buyers who were hoping to be in a new home for the holidays may still find themselves in wait-and-see mode, hoping mortgage rates eventually move back into the 6% range," said Jeff DerGurahian, chief investment officer and head economist at loanDepot. However, mortgage rates won't automatically move higher if the Fed raises its benchmark interest rate, DerGurahian said. For example, if the central bank's move aligns with market expectations and signals that inflation is moving in the right direction, Treasury yields could fall — and mortgage rates could benefit, he said. "However, if Fed officials suggest more aggressive tightening still lies ahead, Treasury yields and mortgage rates could face renewed pressure," he said. "And while a hike may not be the holiday gift borrowers were hoping for, there is still a path for mortgage rates to move into the high 6% range before we ring in the new year." items.title: New-home sales post unexpected surge in October
items.description: New-home sales post unexpected surge in October by John Yellig November 25, 2026 The pace of new single-family home sales blew past analyst expectations in October, posting an annual rate of 701,000, the U.S. Census Bureau and Department of Housing and Urban Development said. The consensus estimate was for the pace to decline from 676,000 in September to 670,000 last month. “Even with mortgage rates at their highest since 2023, buyers turned out for homes they could afford,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said. "Builders have kept sales moving by offering lower-priced homes and helping buyers with financing. Heading into winter, how much more of the monthly payment can builders afford to buy down?” October’s results represented a 14.2% increase over September’s downwardly revised estimate of 614,000 sales and a 7.5% gain from the October 2025 rate of 652,000 sales. The median sales price of new homes in October was $391,300, representing declines of 0.3% month over month and 3.2% year over year. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new houses for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September and 4.1% from October 2025. That represented a supply of 8.0 months at the current sales rate. “The contrast with the struggling resale market comes down to what it costs a seller to wait,” Kushi said. “A homeowner with a low mortgage rate can join the sellers’ strike and stay put, especially if moving means accepting a lower price on the current home and a higher mortgage rate on the next one. Builders face a different calculation. New-home inventory edged down to 470,000 in October, and the faster sales pace brought months’ supply down from 9.3 to 8.0.” Read More Related to This Post Case-Shiller: Miami home-price growth jumps in September What's driving seller confidence in 2026 Miami-Dade home sales post gains YTD through October as interest rates continue to slow deal flow October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle Bleak house: Builder confidence hits 14-year low in November Existing-home sales miss estimates in October Cotality: Northeast, Midwest drive US home-price growth in September Case-Shiller: Miami home-price growth jumps in August Join the conversation Cancel reply Cancel reply Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment.

items.title: Jason R. Armengol
items.description: Jason R. Armengol Property Coordinator Franklin Street, Coral Gables November 25, 2026 What was your most interesting job before going into real estate? I worked as a cameraman filming high school football for a company that provided scouting services. It was an interesting way to experience the game because I was documenting footage that would be used to evaluate players. Where did you grow up? I grew up in Miami-Dade County and have a strong connection to Coral Gables, where I attended high school and where my grandparents live. The area has been part of my life personally, and now it is also where I work. Growing up, what did you want to be? I was drawn to the idea of becoming a businessman. I liked the thought of building a career that involved people, important decisions and opportunities to keep growing. Real estate eventually gave that interest a more specific direction. What do you do to relax when you’re stressed? I like to step away from my phone and give myself some quiet time. I’ll occasionally listen to music or turn on a TV. A walk or a good meal can help me reset. Sometimes a little distance allows me to return to a problem with a clearer perspective. If you could meet any well-known figure (living or not), who would it be and why? George Merrick. Working in Coral Gables makes me curious about the vision behind it. I would ask how he approached creating a city with such a recognizable identity and what he would think of how it has evolved. Where is South Florida's best-kept secret? The residential streets around the Biltmore in Coral Gables. The tree canopy, architecture and quieter surroundings offer a different experience from the South Florida people usually see in photographs. It is a place to slow down and appreciate the details. What do you love most about the industry? The variety of perspectives it offers. My background includes residential brokerage, investment sales support and commercial property management coordination. Each area has taught me something different about properties and the people involved with them. I enjoy connecting those experiences and contributing to a team’s success. What is the most difficult aspect of your job? Keeping competing priorities moving while maintaining accuracy. Property coordination, accounts payable, tenant documents and vendor contracts all require a different kind of attention. Staying organized matters, but so does communicating clearly when priorities change or information is missing. What's your best advice for generating new leads? Listen carefully and follow up with a purpose. Maintaining an organized database helps, but relationships develop through useful conversations and consistent effort. Share information that fits someone’s needs, remember what matters to them and stay connected even when they are not ready to transact. What are you binge-watching/reading/listening to lately? Much of my reading currently revolves around my business coursework at Florida National University. Working while studying makes the material more relevant because I can connect it to professional situations. Outside of school, I gravitate toward content about real estate and career development. What's your favorite meal in South Florida? Churrasco steak, white rice and a Coke. That would be my choice without much deliberation Architecturally speaking, what is your favorite building in South Florida? The Marquis at 1100 Biscayne Blvd. Early in my real estate career, I gained experience selling and leasing units there overlooking Biscayne Bay. The building stands out to me because of its views and the personal connection to that stage of my career. What's the weirdest thing that's ever happened to you on the job? No single incident comes to mind. Having worked across different areas of real estate, I have learned that people and circumstances can make even a routine assignment unexpected. Staying adaptable is part of the job. What's one thing people might be surprised to learn about you? I am completing my bachelor’s degree in business administration at Florida National University while working full time, with graduation anticipated in spring 2027. Balancing both requires discipline, but I appreciate developing my education and practical experience together. What's your favorite vacation spot and why? Orlando and Puerto Rico are the two places I associate most with vacations growing up. I visited both often, so they stand out because of the childhood memories attached to them. In 10 words or less, what is your advice for someone new to the industry? Prioritize education, find the right culture, and work hard. Who are your favorite people to follow on social media? I enjoy following people on LinkedIn whose careers span different areas of commercial real estate. Their experiences can give me a fresh perspective on the industry and introduce me to career paths or ways of approaching the work that I might not otherwise encounter. items.title: D.R. Horton's CEO says the giant homebuilder isn't betting on lower mortgage rates in 2027
items.description: Today’s letter is brought to you by Prophetic ! Land acquisition still runs on spreadsheets, cold calls, and gut instinct. Prophetic gives homebuilders and land teams one AI-native platform for sourcing, feasibility, and outreach, with every deal tracked in a single pipeline. It also surfaces off-market land before it's ever listed, so you can find sites your competitors don't even know exist. Teams on Prophetic move faster from first look to signed contract, so the best parcels don't end up in someone else's pipeline. Curious what that looks like on your own market? See it in action. D.R. Horton closed out fiscal 2026 with around 84,000 homes closed—roughly in line with the reduced guidance it issued last quarter. For fiscal 2027, D.R. Horton guided to 79,000 to 84,000 homes closed—wider ranges than usual, given the uncertainty. The message from management: the nationally aggregated housing market remains soft heading into 2027. During their last earnings call, D.R. Horton’s management said that guidance assumes mortgage rates stay around the recent range. Any sales upside on performance next year, in D.R. Horton’s view, is more likely to come from improving consumer sentiment—a calmer geopolitical backdrop, lower gas prices—than a material decline in long-term interest rates/mortgage rates. Executives described today's buyers as interested but cautious and tentative, held back by affordability and negative headlines. [ ResiClub members can read our 12-chart deep dive on D.R. Horton here ] "I think that anticipating [mortgage rates] to go down isn't prudent at all. So as we look at our guide for the year [we] expect that we're going to continue to see elevated rates. We'll see how that progresses through the spring… and what happens with consumer confidence. If we see some stability in the geopolitical environment, we see some reduction in gas prices and some other things that bring that back, we think that'll help with the market, but [we're] not expecting to see much reduction in rates in the near term." Right now, most economic models (and forward-looking market bets) don’t expect a significant short-term decline in mortgage rates unless something material shifts in the economy (e.g., a spike in the unemployment rate or the AI buildout losing momentum). Fannie Mae’s latest forecast projects the 30-year fixed mortgage rate to average 7.20% in Q4 2027 . Wells Fargo’s latest outlook similarly sees the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaging 6.85% in Q4 2027 . The Mortgage Bankers Association forecast the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate to average 7.10% in Q4 2027 . Keep in mind that forecasts for long-term yields—including mortgage rates—shouldn’t be taken as guaranteed given nailing them also takes getting so much right about the underlying U.S. economy. There’s a lot that goes into financial markets pricing long-term yields/mortgage rates —and if the broader macro picture shifts, so can long-term yields/mortgage rates. Another thing to keep in mind is that even if these forecasts come fairly close to reality, weekly average 30-year fixed mortgage rate readings could still swing above or below the quarterly projected averages. After all, a ResiClub analysis of Freddie Mac’s weekly mortgage rate dataset (see above) finds that since 1972, the average annual range in the 30-year fixed mortgage rate has been 1.40 percentage points (140 bps). Narrowing the window to this century (since 2001), the average annual range has been 1.08 percentage points. In 2025, the spread between the year's highest and lowest weekly readings was 0.87 percentage points (87 basis points). In 2026 (not included in the table above because the year isn't over yet), the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate in Freddie Mac's weekly series has ranged 142 basis points, from a low of 5.98% to a high of 7.40%. Homeownership comes with a lot of responsibility that renters never had to think about. For many Gen Z and millennial buyers, that's a real barrier. "1 in 10 millennials actually doesn't know the difference between a flathead and Phillips screwdriver," Paul Koop , CEO of Builder Backed, said at ResiDay 2026 in New York City earlier this month. Builder Backed is trying to close that gap. The Cincinnati-based company partners directly with homebuilders to act as a concierge after closing. It uses each home's plot plans, blueprints, and HOA documents so owners can get quotes from local contractors and pay for the work inside their builder's app. Owners use it for first-year customizations like fences, blinds, and wainscoting, and for ongoing maintenance like HVAC and lawn care. The service stays with the house. Builder Backed spent the past few years developing the model with Fischer Homes—America’s 32nd largest homebuilder. Fischer's sales teams have pointed to specific deals where it helped them win over buyers choosing between builders. Up to 30% of Fischer homeowners have opted in, and the company is aiming for more than 50%. Koop also said Builder Backed is now ready to expand to other builders and can launch in a new market in under 30 days. Koop thinks builders can eventually follow the auto industry's Lexus playbook: build the home, service it, and resell it under a brand buyers recognize. items.title: Unsold completed new-build inventory is so high more homebuilders are turning to mom-and-pop investors—now it's Dream Finders Homes
items.description: Today’s ResiClub letter is brought to you by Algoma ! Generate the site plan and see how it stacks up to the market in a click. In Algoma , comps and communities are mapped around your site and just a click from capacity: live rent and recent sales by type, size, lot or beds, plus the communities active and coming soon around your site. Don’t just plan your site around zoning and topo, plan around what sells and stands out to your buyers. Complete diligence, all in one platform. Don’t leave homes unbuilt, or unsold. Bring us a site and we’ll run it live in Algoma . As public homebuilders work to clear elevated levels of unsold completed inventory in softer Sun Belt housing markets, they're not only leaning on sales incentives for homebuyers. Some are also stepping up efforts to attract the housing market's biggest investor group: mom-and-pop landlords. Last year, it was Lennar, which launched the Lennar Investor Marketplace in August 2025 . Now it's Dream Finders Homes (America’s 14th largest homebuilder), which recently bought Beazer Homes (America’s 21st largest homebuilder). On November 18, Dream Finders—which is now America’s 7th largest homebuilder after buying Beazer—launched Dream Finders Marketplace , a free website that gives investors access to what the builder calls "investment-ready homes." At launch, it features ready-to-rent homes in 22 cities and communities where Dream Finders builds: the Washington, D.C., metro area; the Raleigh, Charlotte, and Wilmington areas of North Carolina; Myrtle Beach, Greenville, and Spartanburg in South Carolina; suburban Atlanta and the I-85 corridor in Georgia; Jacksonville, Winter Haven, Dade City, and Sarasota in Florida; suburban Nashville; Austin, Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio in Texas; Denver and Fort Collins in Colorado; and suburban Phoenix. Prices range from the high $100,000s to the $600,000s. “With Dream Finders Marketplace, individual investors have a smarter way to invest in new-construction homes… The platform gives individual investors a way to evaluate our homes using the metrics they choose, whether it’s rental comparisons, school district scores, occupancy mix or projected return on investment—all before they ever tour the home. Dream Finders Marketplace gives us another opportunity to connect with new buyers across the U.S. while broadening housing availability, so more people can enjoy a backyard, more space and the other benefits of living in a home.” The site also shows the deals Dream Finders is currently offering, such as a 5.99% interest rate made possible by a builder-paid forward commitment that buys down the market rate. Dream Finders' new investor marketplace comes as unsold completed single-family new construction remains elevated, even as builders continue trying to work it down. To put the number of unsold completed new single-family homes into better historic context, we have the ResiClub Finished Unsold New Homes Supply Index . It accounts for unsold completed inventory relative to new home sales. A higher index score indicates a softer national new construction market with greater supply slack, while a lower index score signifies a tighter new construction market with less supply slack. Over the past few months, that reading has almost drifted back down into the “historically normal” range—however, it’s still on the high side of “normal.” While there's more slack in the new construction market than a few years ago, it isn't evenly distributed. The greatest softness, in both unsold resale inventory and unsold completed new homes, remains in pockets of the Southeast, Southwest, and Mountain West. In particular, it's in parts of Texas, Colorado, and Florida, where active inventory still exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip. Much of that housing market weakness/softness right now is on Dream Finders' home turf. Before the Beazer deal, Dream Finders primarily built in the South. Its heaviest concentration was in Florida. It also had a meaningful presence across the Carolinas, Texas, Tennessee, Colorado, and Georgia. The marketplace's launch list largely tracks that core footprint: Jacksonville, Sarasota, Austin, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, suburban Nashville, and Denver, among others. Many of those are the same markets where builders have had the hardest time moving finished spec homes. With Beazer, Dream Finders now has a much larger footprint. Dream Finders closed 8,608 single-family homes in 2025, according to Builder Magazine, and Beazer closed 4,427. Together, that's 13,035 homes, enough to make the combined company the nation's No. 7 largest homebuilder on a pro forma basis. Among the 15 major homebuilders ResiClub tracks most closely , Dream Finders (14.2%) and Beazer (13.6%) posted the second- and third-lowest homebuilding gross margins in Q2 2026. Only K. Hovnanian (11.8%) was lower. "Margins remain under pressure, and we continue to carefully balance sales pace and price," Zalupski said in the company's Q3 earnings release . It's fair to say builders like Dream Finders are eager to find ways to prevent further margin compression. There's another detail in that release that helps explain the new marketplace. Dream Finders' Q3 net sales fell 15% year-over-year to 1,712 homes. Excluding built-for-rent activity, net sales actually rose 6%, meaning the decline came from bulk sales to build-to-rent buyers pulling back. These regional home price declines raise the question: How many mortgage borrowers currently have negative equity and are actually "underwater"? Amortization of ultra low mortgage rates. Many homeowners locked in ultra-low mortgage rates during the Pandemic Housing Boom. With fixed rates around 2% to 3%, those monthly payments included a larger proportion of principal repayment from the start. That means borrowers have been paying down their balances more aggressively than they would under higher-rate loans. On stage at ResiDay 2026 in New York City on Friday, November 6, Jacobs— America’s 98th wealthiest person according to Forbes —made clear the roll-up is far from over. "We're nowhere near done," Jacobs—who has now formed eight different billion-dollar firms throughout his career—told me on stage. Over the course of our conversation, Jacobs also discussed the soft housing market, tariffs, the data center boom, and why he thinks AI will reshape nearly every job in the industry. Here's what he said, and what it means for builders. When I first spoke with Jacobs in October 2023 , right as I launched ResiClub, he told me he planned to build a large building products distributor, mostly through acquisitions. That's what he has done. QXO has completed three major deals worth roughly $30 billion combined: Beacon Roofing Supply (now QXO Building Products) Lumber, trusses, and building materials Insulation distribution and installation "We did exactly what we set out to do," Jacobs said. Jacobs said almost no QXO customer buys everything the company sells, but most buy many of its products. "There's a huge opportunity to cross-sell and provide greater value to those customers by being a one-stop shop," he said. As for what QXO buys next, Jacobs said it will be opportunistic. "Pretty much anything along the spectrum of building products I like," he said. Which categories come next, and in what order, "really is a little bit depending on what's available and at what price." He also left the door open to buying a technology company, something QXO hasn't done yet. At United Rentals, one of his first deals was a software company whose equipment-tracking system became the company's core operating system. "Our strong relationships with production homebuilders are typically rooted in our truss and wall panel capabilities, as well as insulation, where we solve some of their greatest needs," Jacobs said on the call. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the +1.0% YoY increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the +1.3% YoY increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent runup in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. During the Pandemic Housing Boom, housing demand was running so hot—and homes sold so quickly—listings barely even registered as active inventory. Indeed, in October 2021 , there were only 565,707 active homes for sale, according to Realtor.com ’s data series. That was a staggering -53.8% below the 1,208,311 active listings in October 2019 . At the end of October 2020 and October 2021, not a single one of America’s 200 largest metro area housing markets had more inventory than in pre-pandemic October 2019. Fast-forward to the end of October 2026 , and there were 1,183,520 active homes for sale (just -2.1% below pre-pandemic 2019 levels)—and now 105 of the nation’s 200 largest housing markets have more active inventory than they did in pre-pandemic October 2019. Among the nation’s 200 largest housing markets, the table below shows the 105 markets where active housing inventory for sale at the end of October 2026 exceeded the levels those respective markets had in October 2019. While this data cut (active inventory in a market compared to the same month in pre-pandemic 2019) will slowly become less useful over time, it remains useful right now. One of the common pushbacks I hear when comparing today’s active inventory for sale to 2019 levels is that some markets—like Tampa and Colorado Springs—have larger populations now than they did back in 2019. It’s true that some of the markets with higher inventory today compared to 2019 are also the ones that have experienced notable population growth in recent years. However, that actual population growth—i.e., a larger population base—isn’t the primary reason inventory has jumped so quickly in places like Tampa and Colorado Springs after the Pandemic Housing Boom ended. Rather, it’s because those markets have experienced a sharper weakening in their for-sale market since the Pandemic Housing Boom fizzled out and that has helped push up unsold inventory in those markets. This dynamic isn’t unusual. Growth markets that run hotter during housing booms often experience more pronounced cyclical cooling on the back end. As is often the case, stretched fundamentals, decelerated domestic migration, and elevated levels of new construction coming online—combined with an affordability-shifted market—collectively drive a larger supply-demand equilibrium shift. That said, over time, changes in market size—specifically population and total households—will naturally affect what constitutes a “normal” level of active inventory in higher growth markets (like the Dallas metro area). By 2032, for example, comparing active inventory to 2019 levels will be far less meaningful than it has been in 2021-2026. To get ahead of the "inventory compared to the same month in 2019" metric slowly losing its usefulness, ResiClub has started also using a inventory-per-1,000-household-residents cut (which we already keep in the ResiClub Terminal ) when doing our comparison since pre-pandemic 2018-2019. items.description: Freddie Mac: AI investment Volatility Prompts Rates to Pull Back By Danielle Hale Nov 25, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year fixed mortgage rate pulled back 7 basis points this week to 7.21%, recovering some of the previous-week’s jump that brought rates to 7.28%, as the 10-year Treasury yield has fallen back below 5%. The AI investment trade has created volatility in financial markets as investors try to value companies amid a whiplash-inducing news cycle that included, among other topics, the Anthropic IPO which gave the company a valuation greater than every home currently listed for sale . We’ve already seen AI-generated wealth shape consumer housing behavior, via higher down payments higher in the San Francisco Bay area and other tech hubs . The debate is not whether the Fed hikes in December, but how aggressively it moves. What does this mean for the housing market? items.title: Judge Upholds Mamdani’s NYC Rent Freeze, Tosses Landlords’ Lawsuit
items.description: A Manhattan judge has upheld New York City 's rent freeze for roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments , dismissing a lawsuit brought by landlords who argued that the decision was politically predetermined. In a 20-page ruling issued on Wednesday, New York Supreme Court Justice Brendan T. Lantry found that the city's Rent Guidelines Board had acted within its authority when it voted this summer to freeze rents on both one- and two-year leases. The landlords, led by Kenilworth Holdings LLC, argued that Mayor Zohran Mamdani had effectively dictated the outcome after campaigning on a promise to freeze rents and appointing board members who supported the policy. Judge criticizes Mamdani but upholds freeze Despite the favorable ruling, Lantry wasn't entirely sympathetic to the mayor. In his final decision, he called Mamdani's campaign promise "reckless and irresponsible." Even so, he concluded that the board had independently considered the evidence before reaching its decision. Loading... Mayor Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze is a central piece of his housing affordability agenda, alongside his Block by Block plan to build 200,000 affordable homes and preserve another 200,000 over the next decade. NYC Mayor's Office The freeze passed in June after a landmark 7-1 vote , with only Arpit Gupta , an economist who was appointed to the board in 2022 by Mayor Eric Adams , voting no. But it was owner-representative Maksim Wynn 's statement that stoked controversy at the meeting, after he raised concerns about the financial health of the city's buildings. Wynn's full statement was drowned out by boos from the crowd before he ultimately voted in favor of the freeze. Those pressures were central to the landlords' suit, which argued that a "rent freeze is impossible to reconcile" with such rising costs, pointing to mounting expenses for insurance, maintenance, utilities, and property taxes. Operating and maintenance expenses consumed roughly 71 cents of every dollar of revenue in 2024, according to the board's 2026 Income and Expense Study. And as Realtor.com® previously reported, those figures exclude mortgage payments and major capital expenses, which landlords argue can leave otherwise profitable-looking buildings struggling financially. “Freezing rent sounds like a sure-fire way to solve housing affordability, but what I'm worried about is the unintended consequences on the rent-stabilized stock and market-rate prices,” Jake Krimmel , s enior economist at Realtor.com , said in June. Lantry acknowledged that potential fallout, writing that the freeze could have "detrimental impacts on the New York City residential real estate industry." But he emphasized that weighing the wisdom of the policy was not the court's role, writing that the freeze "has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid." The ruling leaves the freeze intact; however, the landlords could seek to appeal. Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

items.title: Infamous ‘Hoarders’ Mansion in North Carolina Sells for $3.85 Million After Jaw-Dropping Restoration
items.description: A stunning 1929 English Tudor home in Greensboro, NC, that gained notoriety after it appeared in "Hoarders" closed last week for $3.85 million after two years on the market. The home was built during the Gilded Age for prominent local businessman Julian Price , and designed by New York architect Charles C. Hartmann . The 8,616-square-foot home, found at 301 Fisher Park Circle in Greensboro, has over 30 rooms, including eight bedrooms, six full bathrooms, and two half bathrooms. The Julian Price Home was put on the National Register of Historic Place in 1980, it gained attention in 2017, when it was featured on an episode of A&E’s "Hoarders". The home was owned, at the time, by interior designer Sandra Cowart . She had lived in the home since 1975, and kept the home in pristine condition for years, even giving tours and renting out rooms, according to a 2017 article from the Chicago Tribune . After 2005, she became closed off, became a compulsive collector, and her home was ultimately foreclosed on. The home was purchased out of foreclosure by Eric and Michael Fuko-Rizzo for $415,000, a fraction of the property’s value. The couple transformed the home back to its former glory with their deep knowledge and love of old homes and architecture. “They were great people to re-do it, Eric and Michael. Michael’s energy and knowledge of loving old places is honestly over the top,” listing agent Kay Chesnutt , of Berkshire Hathaway Home Services , told Realtor.com. “Not many people would even consider redoing something or saving something like that.” In addition to its numerous bedrooms, the home has an elaborate butlers' pantry, library, great room, and breakfast room. For sunny North Carolina days, there is also a sunroom and a screened porch. All of the details were restored with intention and care for the home’s history. Loading... Originally built in 1929, the Julian Price House has lived many lives. A hoarding situation required a major restoration, after which the Tudor-style home opened as an inn. Chris Groch Photography “It’s like walking into a magical part of history. The beauty of the details and how they were restored—or, if they had to remove something, they’d replicate it,” Chesnutt described the restoration process. “It is something that should be saved for Greensboro. Anybody that goes into it says ‘Wow,’ because the pictures don’t even do it justice. After the restoration, the Fuko-Rizzos opened the home up as an inn. At times, the home would be rented out in its entirety by families or host community events. It even received visits from stars like Carrie Underwood and Leanne Morgan , according to Chesnutt. “Unwind in our drawing room with a book and glass of wine while observing the detail of the original molded plaster ceiling and fireplace surround,” the inn’s website reads. “However you plan your visit, it is certain that the charm, elegance and restored original details of this 1929 Tudor mansion will captivate and leave you and your guests with lasting memories.” The Fuko-Rizzos listed the home for sale again in August of 2024, for an initial price of $5.25 million. Loading... The restoration involved deep attention to detail, with features of the home that required removal being carefully replaced. Chris Groch Photography Loading... The home maintained its classic architecture and design through elaborate molded plaster ceilings and cozy fireplaces. Chris Groch Photography The property’s operation as an inn is one of the reasons that such a stunning home would remain on the market for two years, Chesnutt said. items.title: Meghan Markle’s Hairstylist Shares Glimpse Into the Family’s Return to the U.K.—Including a ‘Special Moment’ in Her Garden
items.description: Meghan Markle and Prince Harry are settling into life in their new home in the Cotswalds , and according to the Duchess of Sussex's wedding hairstylist, George Northwood , the grass is looking very green in the United Kingdom. Northwood shared a look inside the family's latest digs in a Nov. 22 Instagram post , noting that he and Markle had recently spent quite a bit of quality time together, including a lunch date and a visit to her new property. During an early fall trip to Markle's abode, Northwood said they "picked fruit and vegetables" from her garden. The stylist has recently welcomed a son, seven-month-old Elijah , "who has just started weaning" and is exploring new foods. "She was very excited for all the new flavors he was going to enjoy from the garden," Northwood recalled. "I remember Archie being the same age when we went on tour to South Africa, so it was a lovely circular moment." Later, the duo would head to The Park Restaurant—a New York -inspired eatery just blocks from Kensington Palace. In a blog on the eatery's website , Northwood divulged more about their catchup. Loading... Meghan Markle and Prince Harry returned to the U.K. this summer, and her wedding stylist has shared a glimpse into how the family is settling in. Darren Staples / AFP via Getty Images Loading... The Duke and Duchess of Sussex seem to be enjoying their new life overseas, with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet adjusting well to school. Joe Giddens - Pool/Getty Images "I invited Meghan as she has just come back to the U.K. and, though we have stayed in touch via text, we hadn’t had the chance to have a proper download yet," Northwood said of their lunch date. "Since we last saw each other, she’s had her second baby and I’ve had my first. Catching up was like old times, when we used to have dinner together when I accompanied her on royal tours around the world." Northwood added that Markle—who he refers to as "M"—is a wonderful lunch companion because she is "someone with good chat who enjoys a laugh and, crucially, who wants to share the food so that I get to try a bit of everything." The pals enjoyed sea bass, French fries, and key lime pie. Northwood noted that "Meghan was happy to go along" with his pescatarian diet. He also noted that "there is a lot of baby chat" given his recent "solo surrogacy journey," and that he's picked up plenty of "parenting tips" from the mom of two. Northwood also shared a sweet photo of Markle smiling with his son at her home, posed beside a basket of colorful garden-picked veggies. Markle, 45, and Harry, 42, are reported to be residing in a property on an estate belonging to their close friends, according to the Daily Mail . They first made plans to establish a private residence in the U.K. in August of this year, six years after quitting their roles as working members of the British royal family to relocate to a $14.7 million home in Montecito, CA . Although it was recently reported that the seemingly unexpected move was motivated by visa troubles for Harry—with a US government source telling Page Six "his visa expired and wasn't immediately renewed"—the couple's spokesperson denied the claim, telling Newsweek it is "entirely false." In an October interview with GQ, Harry expressed that the decision was driven by a desire to seek out "opportunities for the family." Loading... "I didn't know how important it was to me. I always thought it was going to be something that we would try and do, but now they’ve been in school for two weeks. They’re loving it and it’s just giving them a whole different experience." He also admitted that "it's nice to be back" on "U.K. soil for longer than a few days or a week here or there." The family plans to stay put for the holidays, marking the children's first British Christmas . During a Nov. 20 appearance on the British morning show, "This Morning," Harry revealed the family's plans for Thanksgiving and Christmas, noting that mother-in-law Doria Ragland will be joining them. "My wife is very good in the kitchen and so is my mother-in-law, so I'll leave that to them," he said, noting that he hopes turkey and gumbo are on the menu. The decision to stay in England for the holidays also comes from a desire to keep things simple during a difficult time for Markle's family, as her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr. , has been indicted in Florida on two counts of possession of child pornography. "Everything going on with her dad is still weighing heavily on her," a source told People . "She wants the holidays to be as quiet and enjoyable as possible for the family. items.title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions
items.description: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for applicability of truth in lending and consumer leasing rules for consumer credit and lease transactions Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Federal Reserve Board For release at 3:00 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan. items.title: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans
items.description: Agencies announce dollar thresholds for smaller loan exemption from appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Federal Reserve Board Office of the Comptroller of the Currency For release at 3:00 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500. The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026. The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases. items.title: Apartment sales plummeted 43% in October
items.description: Apartment sales plummeted 43% in October Values dropped 6.3% YOY during the month, though MSCI suggests price declines may be easing. Published Nov. 25, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Getty Images Dive Brief: After the massive AvalonBay Communities-Equity Residential merger boosted apartment sales in the third quarter, the market came tumbling back to earth in October. Transactions plummeted 43% year over year to $7.6 billion, according to a report that data firm MSCI Real Assets shared with Multifamily Dive. This was the slowest October since 2012, when the industry was still digging out of the global financial crisis. It was also the second straight month of double-digit sales declines, according to MSCI. Still, apartment volume is up 51% year-to-date, driven by the Vivmark deal. Prices also fell in October, dropping 6.3% YOY, which was the steepest annual fall since June 2024. However, the annualized one-month change was -6.4%, which was the smallest decline since Q1 2026 and suggests price declines may be easing, according to MSCI. Dive Insight: Single asset sales fell 43% YOY to $6.8 billion in October, and entity trades dropped 40% YOY to $800 million. “While volume will likely revise upwards, this was a particularly difficult start to the fourth quarter,” MSCI wrote in the report. Garden property transactions and mid- and high-rise sales both totaled $3.8 billion in transactions during the month. For garden properties, that sum marked a 51% decline YOY, and for mid- and high-rise assets, a 31% decline. The apartment sector's $7.6 billion in sales trailed industrial’s $9.3 billion in October, according to a separate MSCI report. Office at $6.5 billion was followed by retail at $6 billion and hotel at $2.9 billion. Retail was the only segment to post a YOY October increase, up 5%. Apartment industry executives blame the increase in the 10-year Treasury for the slowdown in sales throughout 2026. In November 2025, it fell below 4% before eventually rising to more than 5.25% in October 2026, according to CNBC. As that happened, deals were shuttered across multifamily and the broader commercial real estate market. “We've seen the volatility and the increase in Treasuries, which has resulted in these higher financing costs and has created a lot of disruption in the market,” Lili Dunn, CEO and president of Bell Partners, told Multifamily Dive. “So as a result, volume has paused significantly.” If rates remain volatile, Dunn said, well-capitalized owners will wait for stability rather than sell at a discount. However, she is optimistic that deals will ultimately pick up in 2027. “I would say it will be gradual, not a surge,” Dunn said. “There seems to be a good amount of capital ready to invest, and fundamentals are actually attractive.” Click here to sign up to receive multifamily and apartment news like this article in your inbox every weekday. Berkadia has arranged $65.5M in bridge financing from Kayne Anderson for Kimaya’s Ocoee Village Townhomes, a 232-home build-to-rent community in Ocoee, FL. The three-year, floating-rate loan will retire construction debt while the property finishes lease-up and moves toward stabilization. Completed in 2024, the 35.3-acre community has three- and four-bedroom townhomes averaging 1,645 square feet, with private garages and amenities including a pool, pickleball courts and a dog park. Wesley Moczul , associate director at Berkadia, led the financing, supported by senior managing director Mitch Sinberg , managing directors Brad Williamson , Scott Wadler and Matt Robbins, and senior analyst Jacob Kelly . ACQUISITION: Millrose discloses 1,233-home rental portfolio acquired from Lennar. Millrose Properties disclosed in its October 27 quarterly results that it acquired 1,233 completed single-family homes from Lennar across 18 states. The portfolio has an aggregate cost basis of approximately $333M, funded with about $120M of balance-sheet capital and $213M of limited-recourse secured financing. Millrose said it underwrote the acquisition as a standalone rental investment, independent of any future path-to-homeownership initiative. CEO and president Darren Richman highlighted the company’s expanding builder relationships and financing capabilities. The release lists FGS Global’s Stephen Pettibone and Louise Fitzgerald as media contacts. Individual communities and the acquisition closing date were not disclosed. Standard Communities has broken ground on Joyfield Towns at German School, an $88M development of 234 affordable rental townhomes in Richmond, VA. Financing includes low-income housing tax credits, tax-exempt bonds, Citibank, U.S. Bank and city support. Joe Ouellette , Standard’s chief operating officer, said stable, affordable housing can help families thrive. Chief development officer Feras Qumseya emphasized the project’s financing and partnerships; Richmond councilmember Nicole Jones and RRHA CEO Steven Nesmith welcomed its affordable housing benefits. Completion is expected approximately 23 months after the October 20 ceremony. DEVELOPMENT: Center Park delivers first homes at 84-townhome BTR in South Carolina.
